blocks.text: Labour is one of the few events in human physiology that is driven by a true positive feedback loop: each contraction stretches the cervix, stretching the cervix releases oxytocin, and oxytocin makes the next contraction stronger, until the baby is born and the stimulus disappears. A few days later, the same hormone is released again every time the baby suckles. This unit explains how labour begins and how the breast produces and releases milk.

blocks.markdown:
**What starts labour (parturition).** Labour is initiated by a combination of fetal, placental, hormonal and mechanical signals, and the exact trigger in humans is not fully understood. The main elements are:

- **Fetal maturation:** as the fetus matures, its hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis becomes more active, and placental corticotrophin-releasing hormone (CRH) rises steeply late in pregnancy. Fetal cortisol and fetal adrenal androgens increase placental production of **oestrogens**.
- **Oestrogen/progesterone balance:** progesterone keeps the uterus quiescent. In humans, serum progesterone does not fall before labour, but a **functional progesterone withdrawal** (a shift in receptor activity) and a rising oestrogen effect increase uterine sensitivity.
- **Uterine changes:** oestrogen increases the number of **oxytocin receptors** and of **gap junctions** (connexin-43) between smooth muscle cells, so the uterus contracts as a coordinated syncytium. It also increases production of **prostaglandins** (PGF2-alpha and PGE2), which stimulate contraction and **ripen the cervix**.
- **Mechanical stretch:** distension of the uterus by the growing fetus and pressure of the fetal head on the cervix increase contractility and oxytocin release.
- **Cervical ripening:** collagen remodelling and increased hydration soften and thin the cervix under the influence of prostaglandins and relaxin.

blocks.title: Positive feedback
blocks.text: In positive feedback a change in a variable triggers a response that amplifies the original change, driving the system away from its starting point until an external event stops it. In labour the stimulus is cervical stretch and the response is oxytocin release, which strengthens contractions and increases cervical stretch.

blocks.markdown:
**The positive feedback loop of labour (the Ferguson reflex).**

1. The fetal head pushes on the cervix, activating **stretch receptors**.
2. Afferent nerves carry signals via the spinal cord to the **hypothalamus**, which causes the posterior pituitary to release **oxytocin** (made in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei).
3. Oxytocin acts on oxytocin receptors on uterine smooth muscle, producing **stronger contractions**, and also stimulates local prostaglandin production.
4. Stronger contractions push the fetal head harder against the cervix, **increasing the stretch** and starting the loop again.
5. The loop ends when the baby is delivered, the cervical stimulus is removed and oxytocin secretion falls.

**Stages of labour.** The **first stage** runs from the onset of regular contractions to full cervical dilation (10 cm), the **second stage** from full dilation to delivery of the baby, and the **third stage** from delivery of the baby to delivery of the placenta. After delivery, continued uterine contraction (aided by oxytocin) compresses the uterine vessels at the placental site and limits blood loss.

blocks.caption: Progress of the first stage of labour is followed by the rate of cervical dilation in cm per hour.

blocks.title: Projecting progress in the first stage
blocks.prompt: A woman's cervix is 4 cm dilated at 08:00 and 7 cm dilated at 11:00. Assuming the same rate continues, at what time will she reach full dilation (10 cm)?

steps.text: Remaining dilation is 10 - 7 = 3 cm, which takes 3 hours at 1 cm/h.
Full dilation is expected at 11:00 + 3 h = 14:00, though real labour rates vary and are interpreted clinically.

blocks.answer: Full dilation is expected at about 14:00.

blocks.markdown: **The breast and lactation.** The breast contains lobules of milk-secreting **alveoli** (lined by luminal epithelial cells surrounded by contractile **myoepithelial cells**) draining into ducts. During pregnancy the breast is prepared by **oestrogen** (duct growth), **progesterone** (lobuloalveolar development), and **prolactin**, **human placental lactogen**, growth hormone and cortisol. Prolactin from the anterior pituitary **lactotrophs** rises throughout pregnancy, but milk secretion is held back because the high levels of **oestrogen and progesterone block the action of prolactin on the breast**. After delivery of the placenta these steroids fall abruptly, which allows prolactin to act, and milk production (lactogenesis) becomes established over the first few days; before this the breast secretes colostrum, rich in immunoglobulin A and protein.

**Prolactin and oxytocin during breastfeeding.** Suckling stimulates sensory nerve endings in the nipple. The signal travels to the hypothalamus with two effects:

- **Prolactin:** suckling reduces release of **dopamine** (prolactin-inhibiting factor) from the hypothalamus, so prolactin secretion by the anterior pituitary **rises**. Prolactin stimulates **synthesis** of milk (lactose, fat and proteins such as casein), maintaining lactation (galactopoiesis).
- **Oxytocin:** suckling triggers release of oxytocin from the posterior pituitary, causing contraction of **myoepithelial cells** and **milk ejection (let-down)**. This is a neuroendocrine reflex that can also be conditioned by the sight or sound of the infant and inhibited by pain or stress.

Suckling also suppresses GnRH pulses, which causes **lactational amenorrhoea** (partial, temporary protection against pregnancy). Pharmacological dopamine agonists (a teaching example) inhibit prolactin secretion and so suppress lactation.

blocks.caption: Roles of the main hormones in lactation.
rows: Duct growth; with progesterone blocks prolactin action in pregnancy
Lobuloalveolar development; blocks milk secretion during pregnancy
Milk synthesis; rises with suckling (dopamine inhibition removed)
Milk ejection by myoepithelial contraction; uterine involution

blocks.title: Effect of a dopamine agonist in a lactating woman
blocks.prompt: A breastfeeding woman is given a dopamine agonist (pharmacology teaching example). Predict the effects on prolactin, milk synthesis and milk ejection.

steps.text: Dopamine inhibits lactotroph secretion of prolactin, so a dopamine agonist lowers prolactin.
With less prolactin, milk synthesis falls and lactation is suppressed over days.
Oxytocin release and myoepithelial contraction are not directly affected, so milk that is already in the breast can still be ejected on suckling, but the supply declines.

blocks.answer: Prolactin falls and milk synthesis is suppressed; the milk ejection reflex remains intact, so the supply declines over time.

items: Labour is triggered by fetal maturation, rising placental CRH, oestrogen effects, prostaglandins, oxytocin receptors and uterine stretch.
Oestrogen increases gap junctions and oxytocin receptors; prostaglandins ripen the cervix.
Labour is a positive feedback loop: cervical stretch, oxytocin release, stronger contractions, more stretch.
Prolactin makes milk; oxytocin ejects milk; suckling increases both.
After the placenta is delivered, falling oestrogen and progesterone unblock prolactin action.

blocks.title: Prolactin makes, oxytocin ejects
blocks.text: Keep the two lactation hormones separate: prolactin stimulates milk synthesis in the alveolar cells (supply), while oxytocin causes myoepithelial cells to squeeze milk out into the ducts (delivery). Suckling controls both, through opposite changes in dopamine and oxytocin release.

blocks.title: Positive feedback needs a stopping point
blocks.text: A positive feedback loop is self-limiting only because an external event ends it. In labour it ends when the baby is delivered and the cervical stimulus disappears; it is not a mechanism that maintains a normal set point.

points: Labour starts through fetal and placental signals (rising CRH, oestrogen effect, functional progesterone withdrawal), prostaglandin production, gap junction and oxytocin receptor expression, cervical ripening and uterine stretch.
Cervical stretch triggers oxytocin release, which strengthens contractions and increases stretch, a positive feedback loop that ends when the baby is delivered.
High oestrogen and progesterone in pregnancy prevent milk secretion; after placental delivery, prolactin acts on the breast to produce milk.
Suckling reduces dopamine so prolactin rises (milk synthesis) and triggers oxytocin release (milk ejection by myoepithelial contraction).

questions.stem: Which hormone causes contraction of myoepithelial cells to eject milk from the alveoli?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: oxytocin mediates the let-down reflex.
distractorRationale.b: Prolactin stimulates milk synthesis but not ejection.
distractorRationale.c: Oestrogen promotes duct growth and inhibits milk secretion during pregnancy.
distractorRationale.d: hPL contributes to breast development in pregnancy but not milk ejection.

questions.explanation: Suckling triggers oxytocin release from the posterior pituitary; oxytocin contracts myoepithelial cells around the alveoli and ducts and ejects milk. Prolactin governs synthesis rather than ejection.

questions.stem: Prolactin levels are high in late pregnancy, but the breast does not secrete abundant milk until after delivery. What best explains this?

options.text: High oestrogen and progesterone from the placenta block the action of prolactin on the breast
Prolactin is not secreted until the baby suckles
The breast has no prolactin receptors in pregnancy

questions.correctOptionText: High oestrogen and progesterone from the placenta block the action of prolactin on the breast

distractorRationale.a: Correct: placental delivery removes the steroid block.
distractorRationale.c: Oxytocin is present but is not the issue for milk synthesis.
distractorRationale.d: Prolactin receptors are present; their action is blocked.

questions.explanation: During pregnancy oestrogen and progesterone prevent prolactin from stimulating milk synthesis. When the placenta is delivered, these hormones fall abruptly, and prolactin can then act, so lactogenesis begins over the next few days.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes the positive feedback loop that drives labour?

options.text: Cervical stretch, oxytocin release, stronger uterine contractions, more cervical stretch
Uterine contraction, prolactin release, uterine relaxation, reduced cervical stretch
Rising progesterone, uterine quiescence, reduced oxytocin
Oxytocin release, cervical relaxation, reduced contractions

questions.correctOptionText: Cervical stretch, oxytocin release, stronger uterine contractions, more cervical stretch

distractorRationale.a: Correct: each cycle amplifies the next.
distractorRationale.b: Prolactin is not part of the labour loop and relaxation would be negative feedback.
distractorRationale.d: This would reduce contractions and so is not amplifying.

questions.explanation: Stretch of the cervix by the fetal head causes oxytocin release, which strengthens contractions and pushes the head harder against the cervix. The loop continues until delivery removes the stimulus.

questions.stem: A mother whose baby suckles vigorously finds that little milk flows during feeds on a day of severe anxiety, though her breasts feel full. Which mechanism best explains this?

options.text: Stress inhibits oxytocin release, so the milk ejection reflex is reduced
Stress abolishes milk synthesis immediately by removing prolactin
Stress causes excess oestrogen to block the breast

questions.correctOptionText: Stress inhibits oxytocin release, so the milk ejection reflex is reduced

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the let-down reflex is sensitive to psychological stress.
distractorRationale.b: Milk synthesis does not stop instantly; milk is present but not ejected.
distractorRationale.c: Oestrogen is not elevated by stress in this way.
distractorRationale.d: Suckling lowers dopamine and raises prolactin.

questions.explanation: The milk is made (the breasts are full), but ejection depends on oxytocin-mediated contraction of myoepithelial cells. Pain and stress inhibit oxytocin release, so the ejection reflex is blunted until the mother relaxes.

questions.stem: Suckling reduces hypothalamic dopamine release, so the secretion of prolactin from the anterior pituitary increases.
questions.explanation: Dopamine tonically inhibits prolactin secretion. Suckling lowers dopamine release, so prolactin rises and stimulates milk synthesis for the next feed.

questions.stem: A woman in labour has a cervix 3 cm dilated at 06:00 and 6 cm dilated at 09:00. Assuming the rate of dilation continues unchanged, how many further hours after 09:00 will pass until she reaches full dilation of 10 cm?
questions.explanation: The rate is (6 - 3)/3 h = 1 cm/h. Remaining dilation is 10 - 6 = 4 cm, which takes 4 hours at 1 cm/h. Actual labour is monitored clinically because rates vary between women.

questions.stem: A breastfed infant takes about 150 mL of milk per kg body mass per day. Calculate the daily milk volume consumed by a 4.2 kg infant, in mL.
questions.explanation: Daily volume is 150 mL/kg/day x 4.2 kg = 630 mL/day. Milk synthesis by the alveolar cells under prolactin control adjusts to demand, since frequent suckling increases prolactin and removal of milk sustains production.

questions.stem: Outline the hormonal and mechanical factors that contribute to the initiation of labour, including how the uterus and cervix are prepared.
markingGuide: Fetal maturation: fetal HPA axis activation and rising placental CRH, with fetal cortisol and adrenal androgens increasing oestrogen production
Oestrogen effect rises relative to progesterone (functional progesterone withdrawal), so the uterus becomes more excitable
Oestrogen increases oxytocin receptors and gap junctions (connexin-43), allowing coordinated contraction
Prostaglandins (PGF2-alpha, PGE2) stimulate contraction and cervical ripening (collagen remodelling, softening)
Mechanical stretch of the uterus and pressure of the fetal head on the cervix increase contractility and oxytocin release
Oxytocin from the posterior pituitary strengthens contractions
questions.explanation: Labour results from a convergence of fetal maturation, hormonal changes and mechanical stretch that make the uterus responsive to oxytocin and ready to contract as a unit, while the cervix softens.

questions.stem: Describe the roles of prolactin and oxytocin in lactation, including how suckling controls each and why milk is not secreted in large amounts during pregnancy.
markingGuide: During pregnancy oestrogen and progesterone prepare the breast but block the action of prolactin, so little milk is secreted
After delivery of the placenta these steroids fall, allowing prolactin to stimulate lactogenesis
Prolactin from anterior pituitary lactotrophs stimulates milk synthesis (lactose, fat, casein)
Suckling reduces hypothalamic dopamine release, increasing prolactin
Suckling stimulates oxytocin release from the posterior pituitary, causing myoepithelial contraction and milk ejection (let-down)
Let-down is a neuroendocrine reflex that can be conditioned and is inhibited by stress or pain
Suckling also suppresses GnRH, causing lactational amenorrhoea
questions.explanation: Prolactin controls production and oxytocin controls delivery of milk. Suckling is the sensory input that drives both through opposite effects on dopamine and oxytocin release.

questions.stem: Explain why labour is an example of positive feedback, describing each step, what ends the loop, and how this differs from a negative feedback system.
markingGuide: Fetal head presses on the cervix, activating stretch receptors
Afferent signals reach the hypothalamus, causing oxytocin release from the posterior pituitary
Oxytocin acts on uterine oxytocin receptors, increasing the strength of contractions (and prostaglandin production)
Stronger contractions press the head harder on the cervix, increasing the stretch and triggering more oxytocin: the response amplifies the stimulus
The loop ends only when the baby is delivered and the cervical stimulus is removed, and oxytocin also helps delivery of the placenta and uterine contraction to limit bleeding
Negative feedback opposes a change to maintain a set point, whereas positive feedback amplifies a change and requires an external event to terminate it
questions.explanation: In positive feedback the output reinforces the input, so the system moves rapidly to an end point rather than holding a steady state. This suits an event that must be completed quickly, such as delivery.
